title: Horizons: Initiative
tagline: A full day on the engine room of agile business analysis — what should we build, and in what order? (Ch 6)
audience: Business analysts, product owners and product managers who work on funded initiatives and need to turn strategic intent into a product vision, a customer-centred feature set and a roadmap that learns.

caseStudy.title: Delivered right first time: last-mile reliability
caseStudy.summary: Southern Cross Freight is a fictional national parcel and freight carrier moving around 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots. Only 79% of consignments arrive within their promised delivery window, 9% fail at the first delivery attempt, and receivers and shippers chase status through the contact centre. The target outcome is on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better within 12 months, with 'where is my consignment' calls down 40%. In this course the investment has already been approved (illustratively): throughout the day we turn that funded initiative into a customer-centred product vision, an impact map and an ordered, testable feature roadmap.
caseStudy.disclaimer: Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

participant.bigIdea: The Initiative Horizon is the engine room: strategy goes in, a product that can learn comes out.
participant.overview:
We open with everything you need for the day, assuming no prior Horizons course: the three planning horizons, the running case and the funded outcome. In our (illustrative) case, the portfolio board has approved Option B, phased: a delivery-management platform with a receiver-notification and real-time booking MVP first, then at-risk flagging and dynamic route optimisation. Today we turn that intent into a product.

**Southern Cross Freight** (fictional) moves about 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots; only 79% arrive within their promised window and 9% fail at the first delivery attempt. Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.
objectives: Describe the three planning horizons and what distinguishes them.
Summarise the funded initiative and its strategic outcome.
Identify what carries over from Strategy and what is new at Initiative.

keyPoints.title: What carries over
keyPoints.body: The outcome (≥92% on-time last-mile delivery), the hypothesis, the riskiest assumptions and the stop signals.

keyPoints.title: What's new
keyPoints.body: Customers and users in detail, product boundaries, features, a roadmap and product-level metrics.

keyPoints.title: Feedback gets faster
keyPoints.body: From quarterly business results to fortnightly or monthly product signals.

sections.heading: The three horizons in five lines
sections.body:
- Agile analysis is sized to the decision in front of you, guided by nine principles (STAG US Pursue, Avoid and Embrace).
- Three horizons: Strategy (should we invest?), Initiative (what will we change or build, and in what order?), Delivery (what's the next slice, and is it done?).
- At Strategy, analysts write a solution-free problem statement and an outcome with a baseline.
- They map assumptions, test the riskiest first, and write a lean business case that names what would prove it wrong.
- Today starts where that ends: the money is committed, and the question becomes what to build.

*See also: the standalone **Horizons: Strategy** course covers the investment decision in depth — optional, not a prerequisite.*

sections.heading: The funded initiative
sections.body:
| Item | Carried forward (illustrative) |
|---|---|
| Outcome | On-time last-mile delivery 79% → ≥92% in 12 months; status calls −40% |
| Recommendation | Option B: buy delivery-management platform, integrate with shipper and subcontractor systems via middleware, phased |
| Phase 1 | Receiver delivery-window notification and real-time booking MVP |
| Phase 2 | At-risk flagging and dynamic route optimisation |
| Key insight | The failed first attempt was the default way to find out a receiver wasn't home |
| Decision point | Week 12 — % complete at booking, first-attempt failure rate |

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.heading: From Strategy to Initiative
sections.body:
The primary question at the Initiative Horizon is: **what should we build, and in what order?** The analyst's questions change:

| Strategy asked | Initiative asks |
|---|---|
| Is this worth doing? | Who exactly must behave differently for the outcome to happen? |
| What options exist? | What product or change will we deliver, and what's in and out? |
| What's the value at stake? | Which features deliver the most value soonest? |
| What would prove us wrong? | What signal will each feature produce, and when? |

modules.title: The analyst at the Initiative Horizon
modules.subtitle: Role, the Product Owner partnership, the five outcomes of analysis and the product vision

participant.bigIdea: At Initiative, the analyst helps the team agree what the product is — and, just as importantly, what it isn't.
participant.overview:
If any single horizon defines the contribution of agile business analysis, it is the Initiative Horizon. Here the Agile Business Analyst understands customers, develops the product vision, builds and orders the feature backlog, shapes the roadmap and keeps a steady flow of features ready for delivery.

This block covers the role, the partnership with the Product Owner, the **five outcomes of analysis** that the rest of the day builds, and the first of them you'll draft: the product vision and its boundary.
objectives: Describe the Agile Business Analyst's contribution at the Initiative Horizon.
Differentiate the Product Owner (decision-maker) and Agile Business Analyst (analyst, investigator, facilitator).
Name the five outcomes of Initiative analysis.
Write a product vision and define the product boundary with a context diagram.

keyPoints.title: Features, not stories
keyPoints.body: Initiative produces features, not stories; a vision, not a specification; a roadmap, not a project plan.

keyPoints.title: PO decides, BA analyses
keyPoints.body: The Product Owner is the decision-maker; the analyst makes sure those decisions rest on understanding, not assumption.

keyPoints.title: The product vision
keyPoints.body: A short statement of who it's for, what need it meets, what it is, and how it differs from today.

keyPoints.title: Boundaries
keyPoints.body: In / out / not yet. 'Not yet' is the most useful column — it lets you say no without saying never.

sections.heading: What the analyst does at Initiative
sections.body:
The Agile Business Analyst at this horizon:

1. **Understands customers** — research, personas, empathy maps, journeys, jobs to be done.
2. **Develops the product vision** — with stakeholders and customers.
3. **Builds and orders the feature backlog** — providing the analysis behind the Product Owner's decisions.
4. **Shapes the roadmap** — a directional plan, not a schedule.
5. **Keeps features ready for delivery** — elaborating just ahead of the Delivery Team.
6. **Bridges** the Delivery Team and the wider stakeholder community — and carries learning up to Strategy.

In larger organizations this may be led by senior analysts or product managers; in small teams it sits alongside Delivery work. What matters is that someone does it with skill and intent.

sections.heading: Working with the Product Owner
sections.body:
The relationship works best when the roles are clearly differentiated. The **Product Owner** is the decision-maker, business voice and keeper of priorities. The **Agile Business Analyst** is the analyst, investigator and facilitator who challenges, probes and tests the Product Owner's thinking — not to undermine it, but to strengthen it.

| Area | Product Owner | Agile Business Analyst |
|---|---|---|
| Vision | Owns and communicates | Drafts, tests with stakeholders, sharpens |
| Priorities | Decides | Provides value, risk and dependency analysis |
| Customers | Represents the customer voice | Researches, models journeys, gathers evidence |
| Backlog | Accountable for ordering | Structures, refines, makes items testable |
| Stakeholders | Primary relationships | Facilitates workshops, manages detail |

In smaller teams one person may wear both hats. The point is that both sets of work happen.

sections.heading: The five outcomes of analysis
sections.body:
![The five outcomes of Initiative Horizon analysis: shared understanding of the customer, a compelling product vision, a prioritized feature backlog, a product roadmap, and well-elaborated features ready for delivery, with the course session that builds each](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/initiative-outcomes.svg)

*The five outcomes of analysis — and where today builds each one.*

These are **living artifacts**, updated as the team learns. The rest of today builds each one in turn.

sections.heading: Writing a product vision
sections.body:
A widely used template (paraphrased): *For [target customer] who [need], the [product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [current alternative], our product [key difference].*

**Running case:**

> For receivers who need their freight to arrive when promised, and the depot planners and drivers who serve them, *Right First Time* is a delivery-management service that captures complete consignment data at booking and confirms the delivery window with the receiver before routes lock. Unlike today's knock-and-hope attempts and overnight manifests, it plans around the receiver's own answer and gets consignments delivered on the first attempt.

Test the vision: can a contact-centre officer repeat it? Does it imply the outcome? Does it exclude things?

The vision is a test any proposed feature can be held against: *does this move us toward the vision, or away from it?* Other product vision techniques you can use: a **product vision board**, an **elevator pitch**, or a structured **visioning workshop** with a broad stakeholder group.

sections.heading: Product boundaries and the context diagram
sections.body:
A **context diagram** is one of the first artifacts at this horizon: what is inside the product, what is outside, and which external actors and systems interact with it. It prevents both over-building and the late discovery of missing integrations. A **systems ecosystem map** extends it with data flows and organizational relationships.

For the running case, inside the boundary: booking validation, receiver notification and confirmation, tracking. Outside but interacting: shipper systems, subcontractor driver apps (via middleware), the route planner, the contact centre.

| In | Out | Not yet |
|---|---|---|
| Real-time shipper booking with address validation | Warehouse management | Shipper self-service dashboard |
| Receiver delivery-window notification and confirmation | Linehaul scheduling | Dynamic route optimisation (phase 2) |
| Live consignment tracking for receivers | Pricing and billing | Parcel-locker network |
| Run data handed to subcontractor driver apps via middleware | Replacing subcontractor systems | Multilingual voice notifications |

presenter.openingLine: "If I stopped a depot planner in the yard and asked what this product is for, what would you want them to say?"

beats.label: Role at Initiative
beats.notes: Walk the six contributions; ask which they do now.

beats.label: PO–BA partnership
beats.notes: Decision-maker vs analyst; discuss real tensions.

beats.label: The five outcomes of analysis
beats.notes: Show the visual; point to where today builds each.

beats.label: Product vision and context diagram
beats.notes: Read the running case vision; apply the tests; sketch the context diagram.

beats.label: Activity: vision and boundaries
beats.notes: Pairs or trios; one plays a stakeholder who wants everything in.

beats.label: Shares and debrief
beats.notes: Two visions read aloud; discuss how to say 'not yet'.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
Visions often come out as feature lists. Ask: 'which word in this tells me who it's for?' Have them read each other's visions aloud — clunky ones become obvious.

Use the roleplay for one pair in front of the group if energy allows.

roleplay.line: "If you're not replacing our driver apps, why should subcontractors care?"
roleplay.curveball: "Our per-drop pay and KPIs come from our own scan data — your product will make our completion numbers look worse."
roleplay.move: Acknowledge the pay and KPI concern, show the 'out' column (no replacement of subcontractor systems), and offer to co-design how run data and KPIs are reported in the pilot.

presenter.whatGood: Visions under 70 words that name a customer, a need and a difference from today; boundaries with a meaningful 'not yet'.
presenter.commonFailure: 'Out' column left empty because nobody wants conflict — the fix is to require at least three items and name the stakeholder affected.
debrief: What did you put in 'not yet' that a stakeholder really wants?
Could a front-line officer repeat your vision?
Where does your BA–PO split need clarifying?
presenter.answerKey: Model vision and boundaries as in sections 3–4. Good 'not yet' items defer valuable but non-essential scope (shipper dashboard, dynamic route optimisation) behind evidence from phase 1.

modules.title: Measuring product outcomes
modules.subtitle: Metrics and KPIs: translating strategic measures into product-level outcomes

participant.bigIdea: Product outcomes are the bridge: faster than the strategic outcome, more meaningful than feature output.
participant.overview: The Strategy Horizon set strategic success measures. At Initiative, **Metrics and Key Performance Indicators** translate them into product-level outcomes and feature-level indicators: what measurable change in customer behaviour or business performance each significant feature should produce, and how we'll detect it. Features with defined success metrics are more honestly prioritized, tested and evaluated.
objectives: Distinguish strategic, product and delivery outcomes.
Express product outcomes as observable behaviour changes.
Define a product metric with a data source, baseline and target.

keyPoints.title: Product outcomes are behaviours
keyPoints.body: Shippers book complete data; receivers confirm before route lock; drivers get run data without rekeying.

keyPoints.title: Three owners, three rhythms
keyPoints.body: Portfolio owns the strategic outcome, the PO owns product outcomes, the team owns delivery metrics.

keyPoints.title: The behaviour test
keyPoints.body: If you can't picture someone doing something differently, it's an output, not an outcome.

sections.heading: Three levels of outcome
sections.body:
| Level | Running case example | Who reviews |
|---|---|---|
| Strategic | On-time last-mile delivery ≥92% | Portfolio board, quarterly |
| Product | % of consignments booked with complete, validated data; receivers confirming before route lock | Product Owner, monthly roadmap review |
| Delivery | Notification response rate; drop-off by step | Team, every iteration |

Product outcomes are the bridge: they move faster than the strategic outcome and are more meaningful than feature output.

sections.heading: Writing a product outcome
sections.body:
A usable product outcome has four parts:

1. **Actor** — who behaves differently (receiver, shipper, driver, planner).
2. **Behaviour** — what they do that they don't do today.
3. **Measure** — the metric, its definition and data source.
4. **Target and time** — baseline → target by when.

*Example:* receivers (actor) confirm a delivery window or safe drop before the 5 am route lock (behaviour), measured as % of notified receivers responding, from the notification platform (measure), from 0% to ≥70% by week 8 of the pilot (target and time).

sections.heading: Outputs in disguise
sections.body:
| Written as | Why it's an output | Rewritten as an outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Launch the receiver app | Describes our work | ≥70% of notified receivers confirm before route lock |
| Integrate with subcontractors | Describes a deliverable | Subcontract drivers start runs with complete data, no rekeying |
| Deliver booking API | Describes a feature | ≥60% of pilot consignments booked complete on day 1 |

Worked example from another industry: a hospital outpatient team's output is *'online booking live'*; the product outcome is *'patients reschedule rather than no-show'*, measured by no-show rate per clinic.

activities.title: Link outcomes to metrics
activities.instructions: For your initiative, write one strategic outcome, two product outcomes and one delivery metric for each product outcome. Then set your review rhythm.

participant.aiPrompt: Given the strategic outcome and product vision below, propose two to three product outcomes expressed as changes in customer or user behaviour (actor, behaviour, measure, baseline → target by when). Flag anything I've written that is really an output and rewrite it. For each product outcome, suggest one delivery-level metric the team could see every iteration. Inputs:

quiz.q: A fintech is building digital onboarding. Which is a product outcome?
opts: Customer acquisition cost falls 20% this year
% of new customers who complete onboarding with verified ID in one session
quiz.why: It's a behaviour change at product level that drives the strategic outcome.

quiz.q: Which of these is an output, not an outcome?
quiz.why: Integration is work we do; the outcome is the behaviour it enables.

takeaways: Product outcomes are behaviour changes that drive strategy.
Every outcome names an actor, a behaviour, a measure and a target.
Rewrite outputs until you can picture someone acting differently.

presenter.purpose: Translate strategic measures into product and feature metrics, so features can later be tied to signals.
presenter.openingLine: "The board will look at on-time delivery every quarter. What will *you* look at every fortnight?"

beats.label: Three levels of outcome
beats.notes: Use the table; ask for a product outcome from someone's initiative.

beats.label: Writing a product outcome
beats.notes: Build the four-part example live.

beats.label: Outputs in disguise
beats.notes: Run the table as a quick-fire: output or outcome?

beats.label: Activity: link outcomes to metrics
beats.notes: Individual; 15 minutes.

beats.notes: Chat waterfall of product outcomes; apply the behaviour test to three.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Participants often write outputs as product outcomes; use the 'is it a behaviour?' test relentlessly. Keep the teach brisk so the activity gets its full 15 minutes.
presenter.whatGood: Product outcomes phrased as behaviour changes with a metric and data source.
presenter.commonFailure: 'Launch the app' as a product outcome — the fix: 'who does what differently once it launches?'
debrief: What behaviour must change for your strategy to work?
Which of your outcomes failed the behaviour test first time?
presenter.answerKey: **Running case:** product outcomes — ≥60% of pilot consignments booked with a validated address and receiver contact; ≥70% of notified receivers confirm a window or safe drop before route lock; subcontractors accept ≥90% of run data without rekeying. Delivery metrics — notification response rate; booking validation pass rate; middleware handoff error rate.

modules.title: Time frame, context and feedback
modules.subtitle: Weeks to months, a rolling one-to-three-month window, and the flows between horizons

participant.bigIdea: Only what is needed soon is elaborated in detail; everything further out is held lightly.
participant.overview: The Initiative Horizon operates over **weeks to months**, with a rolling planning window of roughly **one to three months**. It has no single prescribed cadence — its rhythm follows the Delivery Team's needs. It also sits at the centre of the flows between horizons: context down from Strategy, context down to Delivery, feedback up from Delivery, and learning up to Strategy.
objectives: Describe the Initiative time frame and its rolling one-to-three-month window.
Apply wave-based elaboration to the feature backlog.
Trace the four flows of context and feedback through the Initiative Horizon.
Design a review rhythm that ends in decisions.

keyPoints.title: Weeks to months
keyPoints.body: A rolling window of about one to three months — never the whole product upfront.

keyPoints.title: Wave-based elaboration
keyPoints.body: Next one to two iterations: ready. Beyond: understood at feature level. Outer edge: placeholders.

keyPoints.title: Context down, feedback up
keyPoints.body: Strategy context shapes the vision; Delivery feedback reshapes the backlog and roadmap.

keyPoints.title: Never block delivery
keyPoints.body: The backlog must never fall into a state where the Delivery Team lacks well-elaborated work.

sections.heading: Time frame and the rolling window
sections.body:
![A rolling one-to-three-month planning window: features in the next one to two iterations are ready, features beyond are understood at feature level, and features at the outer edge are placeholders](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/rolling-window.svg)

*Wave-based elaboration across the rolling window.*

A common rhythm, loosely synchronized with delivery:

- **Weekly:** product backlog refinement.
- **Monthly:** product roadmap review — outcomes vs targets, hypotheses validated or rejected, roadmap adjusted.
- **As needed:** discovery and planning workshops.

The important thing is not the frequency but the discipline of continuous engagement. The Strategy Horizon's week-12 decision point sits inside this rhythm.

sections.heading: Context and feedback: the four flows
sections.body:
| Flow | What moves | Analyst's job |
|---|---|---|
| Context **down from Strategy** | Investment rationale, opportunity, customer outcomes, constraints, success criteria | Make sure it's clear and current — or the gaps get filled with assumption |
| Context **down to Delivery** | Vision, ordered feature backlog, roadmap, elaborated features | Tell the team not just *what* but *why* and *for whom* |
| Feedback **up from Delivery** | Iteration reviews, adoption, usage, delivery complexity | Translate it into backlog and roadmap decisions |
| Learning **up to Strategy** | Opportunity bigger or smaller; need different; competitor moved | Surface it in a form strategy decision-makers can act on |

Feedback also flows *within* the horizon: interviews, prototype tests and workshops continuously update the team's understanding.

sections.heading: Kinds of feedback
sections.body:
Use a mix — no single source is enough:

- **Behavioural:** analytics, funnel completion, time-in-step.
- **Attitudinal:** usability tests, receiver interviews, driver and shipper feedback.
- **Operational:** first-attempt failure rate, depot dwell time, call volumes.
- **Commercial/financial:** cost per consignment delivered.

For receivers and drivers, include accessibility and safety signals — speed is not the only measure of a good experience.

sections.heading: Leading and lagging signals
sections.body:
The strategic outcome (on-time %) is **lagging** — it moves slowly and late. Product outcomes and delivery metrics are **leading** — they move within weeks and predict the lagging one.

| Leading (weeks) | Lagging (quarters) |
|---|---|
| Notification response rate | On-time last-mile delivery |
| Booking validation pass rate | Cost per consignment delivered |
| Rekeying errors per run | Customer complaints per 1,000 |

If the leading signals aren't moving by the decision point, the lagging one won't either — that's your early warning.

activities.title: Design the monthly initiative review
activities.instructions: In your group, design a 60-minute monthly initiative review for month 2 of the running case. List the agenda items with timings, the evidence each needs (and who brings it), and the decisions the review can make. Include at least one attitudinal source (for example receiver or driver interviews) alongside the metrics.

prompts.label: Decisions this review can make
prompts.placeholder: e.g. reorder Next column, pause a feature, escalate to portfolio

prompts.label: Who must attend — and who must not be the only voice

participant.aiPrompt: For the initiative below, recommend a fortnightly / monthly / quarterly review rhythm with the decisions taken at each. For each product outcome, identify a leading signal (moves in weeks) and the lagging measure it predicts, and propose at least one behavioural, attitudinal, operational and financial feedback source. Initiative and outcomes:

quiz.q: The Initiative Horizon's planning window is roughly…
quiz.why: A rolling window of about one to three months, elaborated in waves.

quiz.q: A feature at the outer edge of the planning window should be…
opts: Held as a placeholder on the roadmap
quiz.why: Only what is needed soon is elaborated; elaborating far-out work is waste.

quiz.q: Which is a leading signal for on-time last-mile delivery?
quiz.why: Response rate moves within weeks and predicts first-attempt success.

takeaways: Weeks to months; a rolling one-to-three-month window.
Elaborate in waves — ready, feature-level, placeholder.
Context flows down; feedback and learning flow up.
Every review ends in a decision.

presenter.purpose: Set the initiative's time frame and feedback rhythm so the roadmap later has something to respond to.
presenter.openingLine: "If your only feedback is the quarterly board report, how many months could you build the wrong thing?"

beats.label: Time frame and rolling window
beats.notes: Show the wave visual; contrast with upfront project planning.

beats.label: The four flows
beats.notes: Walk the table; ask where their flows break.

beats.label: Activity: design the monthly roadmap review
beats.notes: Breakouts of 3–4; month 2 of the running case.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Compare agendas; highlight reviews that end in a decision and feed learning upward.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Protect the breakout time. Groups default to status-update agendas — push them to name the decisions first and work backwards to the evidence.
presenter.whatGood: A review agenda with timed items, named evidence owners and explicit decisions.
presenter.commonFailure: A review that is a status update — the fix: 'what could this meeting decide to stop?'
debrief: What will you look at every fortnight?
Which decision can your review actually make?
presenter.answerKey: **Model monthly roadmap review (60 min):** 10 min product outcomes vs targets (PO, analytics); 15 min hypotheses validated or rejected since last review (BA); 10 min receiver and driver voice — three interview clips or quotes (BA/researcher); 15 min roadmap adjustments (PO decides); 10 min risks, decision-point readiness and escalations. Decisions: reorder Next, stop or pivot a feature, request portfolio decision early.

modules.title: The nine principles at this horizon
modules.subtitle: Seeing the whole product and thinking as a customer

participant.bigIdea: At Initiative, 'think as a customer' stops being a slogan and becomes a journey you can draw.
participant.overview: The nine principles of agile business analysis find some of their richest expression at the Initiative Horizon, where the work is complex, uncertainty is high and decisions are felt for the life of the product. Remember them with the mnemonic **STAG US Pursue, Avoid and Embrace**.
objectives: Apply each of the nine principles to product decisions.
Spot common Initiative-horizon anti-patterns.
Choose one principle to strengthen on your initiative.

keyPoints.title: See the whole product
keyPoints.body: Shipper, depot, subcontract driver and receiver — the product spans organisations.

keyPoints.title: Think as a customer
keyPoints.body: Design for the receiver on a night shift, on a phone, possibly not fluent in English — not for the person in the meeting room.

keyPoints.title: Avoid backlog waste
keyPoints.body: A 400-item backlog is inventory, not analysis. Detail only what's next.

sections.heading: The nine principles at Initiative
sections.body:
| Principle | At the Initiative Horizon | Anti-pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **S**ee the Whole | Hold vision, customer, strategy, capacity and competition in view — including what is *not* on the backlog | Designing only the screens we own |
| **T**hink as a Customer | Discovery, personas, journey and empathy maps, jobs to be done | Personas made up in a meeting room |
| **A**nalyze to Determine What is Valuable | Make value visible; spot features that look valuable but aren't | Ordering by stakeholder seniority |
| **G**et Real Using Examples | Walk a persona through a feature; hypothesis statements and experiments | Abstract capability lists |
| **U**nderstand What is Feasible | Technical, organizational and financial feasibility; Real Options | Discovering integration limits in iteration 6 |
| **S**timulate Collaboration | Discovery workshops, vision sessions, roadmap reviews, refinement | Drivers consulted after design is done |
| **P**ursue Continuous Improvement | Retrospect on product understanding, not just delivery practice | Never asking if our predictions of value are improving |
| **A**void Waste | Elaborate to the detail the backlog position needs — no more | Full backlog of stories written upfront |
| **E**mbrace Uncertainty and Change | Every plan a hypothesis; every roadmap directional | False precision on scope, date and cost |

sections.heading: Thinking as a receiver
sections.body: A receiver may be working shifts, juggling a job and family, using a phone, and has probably already lost a day waiting in for a delivery that never came. Product decisions that follow from that: plain language; a specific window, not 'between 7 am and 7 pm'; one-tap confirm or safe-drop choice; a clear 'what happens next' if they're out; a phone option for those who need it. These aren't nice-to-haves — they drive first-attempt success, which drives the strategic outcome.

sections.heading: When principles pull against each other
sections.body:
| Tension | What it looks like | A way through |
|---|---|---|
| Think as a customer vs avoid waste | Research every actor before building anything | Research the riskiest actor deeply; others lightly |
| See the whole vs understand what's doable | The ideal journey needs systems we don't control | Map the whole, deliver the controllable slice first |
| Get real vs analyse value | Walking every edge case delays ordering | Walk the five most common real consignments, then order |

Worked example from retail banking: a mortgage team mapped the whole broker-to-settlement journey, but delivered only the document-upload slice first — it was the part they controlled and the biggest wait.

activities.title: Anti-pattern spotting
activities.instructions: Look at your initiative through the anti-pattern column. Which two are most present? For each, write the principle it breaks and one corrective action you can take this month.

Identify the three anti-patterns most likely to be present, explain the evidence, and suggest one corrective action for each I could take within a month. Initiative:

quiz.why: Organizations push for false precision here; treat plans as hypotheses and roadmaps as directional.

quiz.q: Why does 'think as a customer' matter for the strategic outcome here?
opts: Designing for the receiver's real context lifts confirmations before route lock, which drives first-attempt success
quiz.why: Receiver confirmation before route lock is a key driver of on-time last-mile delivery.

takeaways: The product spans actors you don't control — map them.
Customer context drives the metrics that matter.
Detail only what's next.

modules.title: Understanding the customer
modules.subtitle: Personas, empathy maps, journey maps, jobs to be done and job stories

participant.bigIdea: You can't change a behaviour you haven't watched happen.
participant.overview: Behind every feature is a customer. **Shared understanding of the customer** is the first outcome of Initiative analysis — and one of the most easily overlooked. You'll build it with five techniques: **personas**, **customer empathy maps**, **customer journey maps**, **jobs to be done** and **job stories**. These are living tools: a persona on the wall referenced in every planning conversation is doing useful work; one filed in a repository is not.
objectives: Create evidence-based personas for key actors.
Capture what a customer thinks, feels, sees, hears, says and does in an empathy map.
Map the current journey and locate the pain points that drive the outcome.
Express the underlying job, and a feature as a job story.

keyPoints.title: Personas from evidence
keyPoints.body: Based on data and interviews, not imagination. Include context, goals, constraints and what success looks like.

keyPoints.title: Journeys reveal leaks
keyPoints.body: Map what each actor does, thinks and feels at each step, plus elapsed time.

keyPoints.title: Actors beyond your walls
keyPoints.body: Shippers, subcontract drivers and receivers don't report to you — and they decide whether the outcome happens.

keyPoints.title: Jobs, not features
keyPoints.body: Customers 'hire' a product to get a job done. The most valuable features serve that job — not what customers say they want.

sections.heading: What a persona is for
sections.body:
A persona is a short, evidence-based portrait of one **actor** whose behaviour your initiative needs to change. It is not a marketing segment and not a wish list. Its job at the Initiative Horizon is to keep the team designing for real people — and to hand the impact map a clear 'success looks like' behaviour.

![Annotated persona card for Mia the receiver, showing seven parts: name and role, context, goals, pain points, constraints, success looks like, and an evidence strip](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/persona-anatomy.svg)

*Anatomy of a persona — seven parts, each traceable to evidence..*

sections.heading: How to build a persona
sections.body:
1. **Choose the actor** whose behaviour matters most to your product outcome (start with one; two or three is plenty for an initiative).
2. **Gather evidence first** — five to eight interviews, analytics, complaints and support logs, observation.
3. **Cluster what you found** into context, goals, pains, constraints and today's behaviours.
4. **Write 'success looks like'** as one observable behaviour — this becomes an impact on your impact map.
5. **Fill the evidence strip** and rate confidence. Any line with no evidence is an assumption to test, not a fact.

![Blank persona template with name and role, quote, six content boxes and an evidence and confidence strip](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/persona-template.svg)

*Persona template — download the printable PDF from Resources.*

sections.heading: Running case personas
sections.body:
**Mia, 34, shift-working nurse (illustrative).** Ordered a 30 kg flat-pack wardrobe online. Mostly uses her phone. Already missed one delivery while on a night shift. Wants: to know when it will arrive, or where it can be left. Constraint: can't take calls on the ward; English is her second language.

**Ravi, dispatch coordinator at a mid-sized online retailer (the shipper).** Books consignments from a spreadsheet a few times a day. Unsure of cut-offs and address rules. Wants: a clear, quick booking. Constraint: dispatch is only part of his job.

**Jess, route planner at a Southern Cross Freight depot.** Rekeys addresses that fail validation before the 5 am route lock. Wants: complete, confirmed data before planning. Constraint: subcontractor systems and per-drop KPIs.

Each persona should state the evidence it's based on (data, interviews, complaints).

sections.heading: Customer empathy maps
sections.body:
An empathy map captures what the customer **thinks and feels**, **hears**, **sees**, **says and does**, plus the **pains** and **gains** that shape their experience. Build it from real research — interviews, observation, contextual inquiry — not imagination.

![Customer empathy map for Mia the receiver with quadrants for thinks and feels, hears, sees, says and does, and a pains and gains strip](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/empathy-map.svg)

*Empathy map — Mia, the receiver. A blank template is in Resources.*

sections.heading: How a journey map works
sections.body:
A journey map follows **one persona through one scenario**, stage by stage. Read across a row for the story; read down a column for everything happening at that moment. The emotion curve and the elapsed-time row usually show where the outcome leaks.

![Explainer of a journey map grid with rows for stages, does, thinks, feels, elapsed, pain and opportunity, and six build steps](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/journey-how-it-works.svg)

*How a journey map works — the seven rows and six build steps.*

| Row | Ask | Common mistake |
|---|---|---|
| Stages | What phases would the actor name? | Using your internal process steps |
| Does | What do they physically do? | Writing what the system does |
| Thinks | What are they wondering? | Leaving it blank |
| Feels | Up or down at this moment? | Making every step neutral |
| Elapsed | How long, and how long waiting? | Ignoring waits between steps |
| Pain | What breaks? | Listing every annoyance equally |
| Opportunity | What might fix the biggest pain? | Jumping to one solution too early |

sections.heading: Running case journey
sections.body:
![Mia's current delivery journey across five stages: order, dispatch, wait, attempt, recover, with the emotion curve dipping lowest at the failed attempt](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/journey-worked-example.svg)

*Worked example — Mia's journey. The deepest dip is the failed first attempt.*

| Step | Receiver does | Feels | Elapsed (illus.) | Pain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Order | Buys online, gets 'ships in 1–2 days' | Hopeful | Day 0 | No delivery day given |
| Dispatch | Gets generic dispatch email | Uncertain | Day 1 | Tracking says 'in transit' only |
| Waits | Nothing visible | Frustrated | Day 1–3 | Can't plan around shifts |
| Attempt | Not home; card left | Annoyed | Day 3 | Nobody asked beforehand |
| Re-delivery or collection | Drives to depot | Resigned | Day 5–6 | Too heavy for her car |

The 'attempt' row is the default-discovery insight, now felt from the receiver's side.

Your turn: use the blank template below for the persona you chose.

![Blank journey map template with six stages and seven rows](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/journey-template.svg)

*Journey map template — download the printable PDF from Resources.*

sections.heading: Jobs to be done and job stories
sections.body:
**Jobs to be done** asks what job the customer is hiring the product to accomplish. Mia isn't hiring 'delivery notifications' — she's hiring *'get my wardrobe without losing a shift'*.

A **job story** frames a feature around the situation that motivates it:

> *When* I'm working nights and a big delivery is due, *I want to* choose a safe place or a window that fits my roster, *so I can* get it first time without swapping a shift.

| User story | Job story |
|---|---|
| As a receiver, I want SMS notifications | When a delivery is due and I can't be home, I want to choose what happens, so I don't lose a day |
| Role + capability | Situation + motivation + expected outcome |

Job stories keep features anchored to motivation rather than to a surface-level request.

modules.title: Connecting features to outcomes
modules.subtitle: Impact mapping and opportunity solution trees

participant.bigIdea: An impact map turns 'we're building a front door' into 'here's whose behaviour we're changing and why'.
participant.overview: Two techniques connect what we might build to why. **Impact mapping** links the goal to actors, the behaviours we need from them and the features that support those behaviours. **Opportunity solution trees** link a product outcome to the opportunities that could produce it and the solutions that could address each opportunity — making sure the solution space is explored before committing.
objectives: Build an impact map: goal → actors → impacts → deliverables.
Express impacts as measurable behaviour changes.
Move deliverables that can't justify an impact to 'not yet'.
Build an opportunity solution tree to widen the solution space.

keyPoints.title: Impact maps connect why to what
keyPoints.body: Goal (why) → actors (who) → impacts (how behaviour changes) → deliverables (what).

keyPoints.title: Read it right to left
keyPoints.body: Every deliverable must justify itself through an impact on an actor that moves the goal.

keyPoints.title: 'Not yet' is a decision
keyPoints.body: Deliverables without a clear impact wait for evidence — they aren't deleted, they're deferred.

sections.heading: Impact mapping
sections.body:
```
GOAL: On-time last-mile delivery ≥92%
├── Receiver (Mia)
│   ├── Impact: confirms availability or a safe drop before route lock
│   │   ├── Deliverable: SMS/email notice with one-click confirm or safe drop
│   │   └── Deliverable: plain-language delivery window
│   └── Impact: stops calling to check status
│       └── Deliverable: live tracking with SMS updates
├── Shipper (Ravi)
│   └── Impact: books with validated address and receiver contact on day 1
│       └── Deliverable: real-time booking API with address validation
└── Depot planner and driver (Jess)
    └── Impact: plans and delivers runs without rekeying or futile attempts
        ├── Deliverable: complete run data via middleware to driver apps
        └── Deliverable: at-risk flag at sort
```

Read it right to left: every deliverable must justify itself by an impact on an actor that moves the goal. Deliverables that can't do that are candidates for 'not yet'.

sections.heading: Checking the map
sections.body:
Run four checks before you call it done:

1. **External actors** — at least one actor outside your organisation.
2. **Measurable impacts** — each impact could be counted.
3. **More than one deliverable option** per impact — otherwise you've reverse-engineered a solution.
4. **A 'not yet' margin** — at least one deliverable lost its place.

Worked example from higher education: a university's goal was first-year retention. The impact 'students book an adviser in week 3' had three options — SMS nudge, timetable slot, peer mentor. The planned app was moved to 'not yet'.

sections.heading: Opportunity solution trees
sections.body:
```
OUTCOME: ≥70% of notified receivers confirm before route lock
├── Opportunity: receivers don't know a delivery is coming
│   ├── Solution: SMS/email notice the evening before
│   └── Solution: retailer checkout asks for preferred window
├── Opportunity: receivers can't be home in the window
│   ├── Solution: one-tap safe-drop choice
│   └── Solution: redirect to a nearby pickup point
└── Opportunity: receivers don't trust unknown senders
    └── Solution: notice branded with the retailer's name
```

Read it top down: outcome → opportunities (customer needs, pains or desires found in discovery) → solutions. Several solutions per opportunity is the point — it stops the first idea becoming the only idea. Pick solutions to test with **hypothesis statements** (session 2.9).

| | Impact map | Opportunity solution tree |
|---|---|---|
| Starts from | Goal | Product outcome |
| Organizes by | Actors and their behaviour | Customer opportunities |
| Best for | Many actors, cross-organization products | Deep discovery on one customer group |

activities.title: Impact map (or opportunity solution tree)
activities.instructions: Build an impact map for your initiative (or the running case): at least three actors, one or two impacts each, and deliverables under each impact. Circle deliverables that cannot justify an impact. If your product serves one main customer group, you may build an opportunity solution tree instead.

quiz.why: It keeps the solution space broad and connected to the outcome.

takeaways: Actors and impacts before deliverables.
Every deliverable must earn its place.
Explore several solutions per opportunity.
'Not yet' is a decision, not a deletion.

modules.title: Story mapping, MVP and feature decomposition
modules.subtitle: The whole journey, the smallest valuable slice, and features broken down for sequencing

participant.bigIdea: The first release should cross the whole journey thinly, not one step of it thickly.
participant.overview: A **story map** lays the user's activities out as a backbone, with alternatives beneath. **Minimum viable product** thinking finds the smallest set of features that delivers the core value proposition and generates real feedback. **Story decomposition** at this horizon breaks large features into mid-level, independently deliverable capabilities that the roadmap can sequence.
objectives: Lay out a story map backbone of 4–6 activities.
Slice a first release that tests the riskiest impact.
Decompose a large feature into mid-level capabilities for sequencing.

keyPoints.title: Story maps slice releases
keyPoints.body: A backbone of activities, with stories beneath, sliced horizontally into releases.

keyPoints.title: Thin and whole
keyPoints.body: A walking skeleton across every step beats a polished single step.

sections.heading: Story mapping
sections.body:
Arrange the receiver's activities as a **backbone** (Order → Get delivery window → Track consignment → Receive delivery), place user stories underneath each activity, then draw horizontal lines to slice releases.

**Release 1 (MVP) for the running case:** receiver delivery-window notification with one-click confirm or safe drop; real-time booking with address validation for pilot shippers; run data to one subcontractor via middleware; basic tracking by SMS. Everything else waits for evidence from Release 1.

sections.heading: MVP and feature decomposition
sections.body:
**MVP** is not 'version one of everything' — it is the smallest set that tests the core value proposition with real customers. For the running case: receiver confirmation, validated booking for pilot shippers, run data to one subcontractor, SMS tracking.

**Decomposition at Initiative** produces features, not stories:

| Large feature | Mid-level features (Initiative) | Stories (later, at Delivery) |
|---|---|---|
| Receiver delivery management | Window notification · one-tap confirm · safe-drop choice · re-book after a miss | Elaborated just in time |

Decompose enough to sequence and release incrementally — not so far that you're writing stories for work six months away.

activities.title: Story map backbone and first slice
activities.instructions: Write the backbone (4–6 activities) and draw your first release slice.

opts: Mid-level features that will be elaborated later
quiz.why: Initiative decomposition is for sequencing; story-level detail waits for Delivery.

takeaways: Backbone first, stories second.
Slice a thin first release across the whole journey.

modules.title: Hypotheses and prioritization techniques
modules.subtitle: Hypothesis statements, Kano, Purpose Alignment, value modelling, MoSCoW, WSJF and collaborative games

participant.bigIdea: A feature without a hypothesis is a guess; a feature with one is an experiment.
participant.overview: Prioritizing the feature backlog is one of the most analytically demanding activities at this horizon. Features compete on customer value, contribution to the vision, technical risk, dependencies and strategic alignment. The analyst makes the trade-offs visible; **the decision belongs to the Product Owner**. First, every feature becomes a **hypothesis statement**; then we order using the right technique for the decision.
objectives: Write hypothesis statements with a measurable signal.
Choose a prioritization technique to fit the decision.
Order features and explain the reasoning to the Product Owner.

keyPoints.title: Feature hypothesis
keyPoints.body: We believe [feature] will result in [impact] for [actor]. We'll know when [signal] reaches [threshold] by [time].

keyPoints.title: Order, don't prioritise
keyPoints.body: Priorities collapse into 'all high'. A strict order forces trade-offs.

keyPoints.title: Learning is value
keyPoints.body: Early features that test the riskiest assumption can be worth more than larger features.

keyPoints.title: PO decides
keyPoints.body: The analysis is the analyst's; the prioritization decision is the Product Owner's.

sections.heading: Hypothesis statements
sections.body:
*We believe that [feature] will produce [outcome] for [customer], and we will know we are right when [measurable signal].*

| Feature | Hypothesis | Signal and threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Receiver delivery-window confirmation | Receivers confirm availability or a safe drop when asked directly | ≥70% respond before route lock |
| Real-time booking with address validation | Shippers book complete consignments on day 1 | ≥60% of pilot consignments complete at booking by week 8 |
| Run data via middleware to subcontractors | Drivers deliver without rekeying or futile attempts | First-attempt failure rate ≤5% |
| At-risk flag at sort | At-risk consignments can be re-planned before dispatch | ≥80% of late consignments flagged; <5% false alarms |
| SMS live tracking | Receivers stop calling for status | Status calls from pilot cohort −40% |

sections.heading: Prioritization techniques
sections.body:
No single technique fits every decision — choose for the context:

| Technique | Question it answers | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Kano Analysis** | Is it basic, performance or delight? | Ensuring basics are covered before polishing; spotting differentiators |
| **Purpose Alignment Model** | Does it differentiate us, or is it necessary but non-differentiating? | Deciding where to invest vs standardize |
| **Value Modeling** | What outcome will it produce, measured how? | Moving from opinion to explicit value |
| **MoSCoW** | Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time)? | Scoping a release with stakeholders |
| **Cost of delay / WSJF** | What do we lose per week, divided by size? | Sequencing a flow of features |
| **Dot voting / Buy a Feature** | What do stakeholders value when budget is limited? | Surfacing honest trade-offs (collaborative games) |

Running case through Kano: delivery-window notice is now **basic** (receivers expect it); one-tap safe drop is **performance**; retailer-branded live map is **delight**. Purpose Alignment: booking validation is necessary but not differentiating — buy or standardize it; receiver confirmation is differentiating — invest.

sections.heading: Ordering the running case
sections.body: In the running case, receiver delivery-window confirmation ranks first: high value, high cost of delay, tests the privacy and response assumptions, modest size. Remember: the analyst prepares the analysis; the Product Owner makes the call.

activities.title: Top five ordered features
activities.instructions: From your impact map or tree, choose five features. Write a hypothesis statement for each, pick one prioritization technique that fits your context, and put the five in strict order with one line of reasoning per position.

participant.aiPrompt: Act as a product analyst. For each feature below, write a hypothesis in the form 'We believe [feature] will result in [impact] for [actor]; we'll know when [signal] reaches [threshold] by [time]'. Then propose a strict order using value, cost of delay, risk reduction and relative effort, explaining each position in one line and noting which assumption each feature tests. Finally lay out a Now / Next / Later roadmap with an outcome per column. Features and context:

quiz.q: Why order features strictly rather than tagging priority High/Medium/Low?
quiz.why: Strict order prevents everything being 'High'.

quiz.q: Weighted shortest job first divides…
opts: Cost of delay by job size
quiz.why: WSJF = cost of delay ÷ size, favouring high-value small items.

quiz.q: In Kano Analysis, a feature whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence goes unnoticed is…
quiz.why: Basic features are expected; cover them before elaborating performance features.

takeaways: Every feature gets a hypothesis and a signal.
Order strictly; reason out loud.
Value learning — test risky assumptions early.

presenter.purpose: Turn the impact map into an ordered, testable feature set and roadmap.
presenter.openingLine: "Five features. One order. No ties. Let's find out what you really believe."

beats.label: Hypothesis statements

presenter.facilitationNotes: Expect resistance to strict ordering. Allow ties for 30 seconds, then insist. Watch for features with no signal.

presenter.commonFailure: Signals that are outputs ('feature released') — the fix: what behaviour will we see?

Which feature was hardest to write a signal for?
presenter.answerKey: Model order: 1 receiver delivery-window confirmation; 2 real-time booking with address validation; 3 middleware run data to one subcontractor; 4 at-risk flag; 5 SMS live tracking. Rationale: 1 tests the privacy and response assumptions and attacks the biggest leak; 2 drives completeness; 3–4 depend on 1–2 data; 5 is valuable but lower cost of delay.

modules.title: The product roadmap and real options
modules.subtitle: A directional plan that tells a story — and decisions held open until the last responsible moment

participant.bigIdea: A roadmap is a statement of intent and learning, not a delivery contract.
participant.overview: The **product roadmap** is the Initiative Horizon's primary communication artifact — a directional plan, not a schedule or a commitment to dates. A good roadmap tells a story: how early deliveries build the foundation, how the product grows from its minimum viable form toward its vision, and how each phase generates feedback. **Real Options** keeps decisions open until the last responsible moment.
objectives: Build a Now / Next / Later outcome roadmap.
Explain how signals move items between columns.

keyPoints.title: Roadmap by outcome
keyPoints.body: Now / Next / Later columns hold outcomes and hypotheses, not dates and feature lists.

keyPoints.title: Columns move on evidence
keyPoints.body: An item moves from Next to Now when the signal it depends on arrives — not when a date passes.

sections.heading: The Now / Next / Later roadmap
sections.body:
| Now (next ~6 weeks) | Next (~6–12 weeks) | Later |
|---|---|---|
| Outcome: receivers confirm before route lock | Outcome: runs delivered without futile attempts | Outcome: dynamic re-planning on the day |
| Receiver confirmation; real-time booking | Middleware run data; at-risk flag | Route optimisation, shipper dashboard |
| Signal: response rate, completeness | Signal: first-attempt failure rate | Signal: on-time %, re-plan rate |

The roadmap is a communication tool; it changes as signals arrive.

sections.heading: Real options
sections.body:
Defer commitment until the point where the cost of not deciding exceeds the value of the information gained by waiting.

| Decision | Option held open | Decide by |
|---|---|---|
| Route optimisation vendor | Keep two vendors in the running | When Release 1 data shows real re-plan volumes |
| Parcel-locker network | Partner pilot vs build | After safe-drop uptake is known |

Ask of each roadmap item: does this decision genuinely need to be made now?

quiz.why: Outcome roadmaps communicate intent and learning, not delivery dates.

quiz.q: Real Options advises committing…
quiz.why: Defer until the cost of waiting exceeds the value of more information.

takeaways: Roadmap by outcome, and change it as signals arrive.

modules.title: Features ready for delivery
modules.subtitle: Story elaboration, the Three Amigos, the Kanban board and relative estimation

participant.bigIdea: The handoff to Delivery works best as a continuous flow, not a gate.
participant.overview: The fifth outcome of Initiative analysis is a steady supply of **features ready for delivery**. A ready feature has a clear user need, an agreed scope and boundary, initial acceptance conditions, and known risks and dependencies — but *not* fully specified stories. That detail comes at the Delivery Horizon, just in time.
objectives: Apply a feature-readiness check.
Use the Three Amigos, a Kanban board and relative estimation to keep elaboration just ahead of delivery.

keyPoints.title: Ready, not specified
keyPoints.body: Need, scope, initial acceptance conditions, risks and dependencies — no detailed stories yet.

keyPoints.title: Three Amigos at Initiative
keyPoints.body: Product Owner, analyst and a Delivery Team member check a feature is understood well enough to decompose and sequence.

keyPoints.title: Make the pipeline visible
keyPoints.body: A Kanban board shows features moving from identified to ready — and where they get stuck.

sections.heading: The feature-readiness check
sections.body:
| Check | Running case: receiver confirmation |
|---|---|
| User need | Receivers can't plan around an unknown delivery window |
| Scope and boundary | Notice, confirm, safe drop; *not* re-booking after a miss (next feature) |
| Initial acceptance conditions | Confirmation reaches the route planner before route lock; works on a phone in plain language |
| Non-functional constraints | Accessibility, privacy of receiver contact data, SMS delivery time |
| Risks and dependencies | Shipper must supply a mobile number; middleware to route planner |
| Size | Relative estimate: M (T-shirt) |

**Non-functional requirements** set at product level here flow down as constraints on every story.

sections.heading: Keeping the pipeline flowing
sections.body:
- **Story elaboration (light touch):** enough to plan confidently, not so much it over-constrains the Delivery Team.
- **Three Amigos:** Product Owner, analyst and a Delivery Team member talk through the feature — is it understood, how complex is it, is the priority grounded in delivery reality?
- **Kanban board:** Identified → Exploring → Elaborating → Ready, with a work-in-progress limit.
- **Relative estimation:** T-shirt sizes or feature points for roadmap sequencing.
- **Spikes:** time-boxed investigations when uncertainty would make planning unreliable.

Watch the Delivery Team's backlog consumption and stay one to two iterations ahead. If a feature turns out larger than expected, decompose it, adjust the roadmap or find a simpler first version.

participant.bigIdea: Leave with a product the team can start building on Monday — and a way to know if it's working.
participant.overview: Consolidate the five outcomes for your own funded initiative, check traceability, and see where the whole Initiative toolkit fits. Then we look at what happens next at the Delivery Horizon.
objectives: Consolidate your five outcomes of analysis.
Check traceability from strategic outcome to feature signal.
Know where the rest of the 43 Initiative techniques fit.

keyPoints.title: Traceability
keyPoints.body: Outcome → actor → impact → feature → signal. Every link should be explicit.

keyPoints.title: Direct the agent
keyPoints.body: Use AI to tidy and cross-check; you own the order.

keyPoints.title: Bring one feature
keyPoints.body: Next, your top feature gets elaborated end to end at the Delivery Horizon.

sections.heading: Exercise brief
sections.body:
1. Customer: persona, empathy map, journey, job story.
2. Vision and boundary (≤70 words).
3. Impact map or opportunity solution tree; mark 'not yet'.
4. Top five ordered, with hypothesis statements; Now / Next / Later.
5. Readiness check on your #1 — the feature you'd take into delivery first.

sections.heading: The Initiative Horizon toolkit
sections.body:
The book lists 37 analysis techniques and 6 planning and delivery techniques for this horizon. Today you practised the ones in bold teal; the rest are your reference toolkit, grouped by the outcome they mainly serve.

![Map of all 43 Initiative Horizon techniques grouped by the five outcomes of analysis, with the techniques taught in this course highlighted](/files/horizons-initiative/visuals/technique-map.svg)

*The Initiative Horizon technique map. Grouping by outcome is this course's; most techniques serve more than one outcome.*

sections.heading: What comes next: the Delivery Horizon
sections.body:
At the Delivery Horizon the question becomes *what's the next most valuable slice, and is it done?* The team takes one feature — for the running case, receiver delivery-window confirmation — splits it into stories, elaborates one with examples, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements and a value metric, and plans the iteration around it.

**See also:** if you want to go deeper on delivery, the standalone **Horizons: Delivery** course spends a full day on exactly this. Optional, and self-contained.
